Propensity Score Adjustment for ForestSearch GLM Extension

Implementation Design and Simulation Evaluation

Author

Larry F. León

Published

March 25, 2026

Show code 
devtools::document(quiet = TRUE)
devtools::load_all(".", quiet = TRUE)
source("dev/glm/glm_effect_estimators.R")

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(survival)
  library(data.table)
  library(grf)
  library(glmnet)
  library(gt)
})

1 Design Overview

ForestSearch’s GLM extension now supports optional propensity score (PS) adjustment for subgroup effect estimation. The PS is included as an adjustment covariate in the GLM estimator closure, adding a doubly-robust flavour to the treatment effect estimates.

1.1 Architecture

The doubly-robust approach follows Bang & Robins (2005): the propensity score \(\hat{e}(X)\) is estimated on the full sample, then the inverse propensity score (IPS) covariate is constructed as \(1/\hat{e}(X_i)\) for treated subjects and \(1/(1 - \hat{e}(X_i))\) for controls. This IPS covariate is included in the outcome GLM, yielding a treatment effect estimate that is consistent if either the propensity model or the outcome model is correctly specified.

forestsearch()
  └── Section 2C: estimate_propensity_scores()
        ├── method = "grf"      →  grf::regression_forest(X, W)
        ├── method = "lasso"    →  glmnet::cv.glmnet(X, W, family="binomial")
        ├── method = "logistic" →  glm(W ~ X, family=binomial)
        └── method = "none"     →  skip (default for RCT)
      ↓
  ps_hat = e(X) estimated on full sample
  ips_covar = 1/e(X) for treated, 1/(1-e(X)) for control  [Bang & Robins 2005]
      ↓
  make_effect_estimator(..., adjust_covariates = "ips_covar")
      ↓
  closure: glm(Y ~ treat + ips_covar, ...)  →  doubly-robust estimate

1.2 Parameter Defaults

Setting ps_method default Rationale
is.RCT = TRUE "none" Randomization ensures balance
is.RCT = FALSE "grf" Non-parametric, cross-fitted
User-supplied PS Pass ps_hat vector Maximum flexibility

1.3 PS Estimation Methods

Method Implementation Pros Cons
"grf" regression_forest(X, W) Non-parametric, OOB cross-fitted Requires grf
"lasso" cv.glmnet(X, W, family="binomial") Penalized, handles many covariates Parametric (log-odds)
"logistic" glm(W ~ X, family=binomial) Simple, interpretable May misspecify
"none" Skip No overhead No confounding adjustment

All methods include PS trimming at [2.5%, 97.5%] quantiles by default to avoid positivity violations.

2 GBSG Demonstration

2.1 PS Estimation Comparison

df <- survival::gbsg
df$id <- seq_len(nrow(df))
df$grade3 <- as.integer(df$grade == "3")
confs <- c("age", "meno", "size", "grade3", "nodes", "pgr", "er")

ps_grf    <- estimate_propensity_scores(df, "hormon", confs, method = "grf")
ps_lasso  <- estimate_propensity_scores(df, "hormon", confs, method = "lasso")
ps_logit  <- estimate_propensity_scores(df, "hormon", confs, method = "logistic")

ps_compare <- data.frame(
  Method     = c("GRF", "LASSO", "Logistic"),
  Mean       = round(c(mean(ps_grf$ps_hat), mean(ps_lasso$ps_hat),
                        mean(ps_logit$ps_hat)), 3),
  SD         = round(c(sd(ps_grf$ps_hat), sd(ps_lasso$ps_hat),
                        sd(ps_logit$ps_hat)), 3),
  Min        = round(c(min(ps_grf$ps_hat), min(ps_lasso$ps_hat),
                        min(ps_logit$ps_hat)), 3),
  Max        = round(c(max(ps_grf$ps_hat), max(ps_lasso$ps_hat),
                        max(ps_logit$ps_hat)), 3),
  Trimmed    = c(ps_grf$trimmed, ps_lasso$trimmed, ps_logit$trimmed),
  Cor_GRF    = round(c(1, cor(ps_grf$ps_hat, ps_lasso$ps_hat),
                        cor(ps_grf$ps_hat, ps_logit$ps_hat)), 3)
)

gt(ps_compare) |>
  tab_header(title = md("**PS Estimation Methods on GBSG Data**"),
             subtitle = "P(hormon = 1 | X)") |>
  cols_label(Cor_GRF = "Cor with GRF")

2.2 Adjusted vs Unadjusted Estimates

The doubly-robust adjustment follows Bang & Robins (2005): the inverse propensity score (IPS) covariate is defined as \(1/\hat{e}(X_i)\) for treated subjects and \(1/(1 - \hat{e}(X_i))\) for controls. Including this as a covariate in the outcome GLM yields consistency if either the propensity or outcome model is correctly specified.

Show code 
df_ps <- ps_grf$data

fn_unadj <- make_effect_estimator("binary", "hormon", "status",
  offset.name = "rfstime", effect_measure = "IRR")
fn_adj <- make_effect_estimator("binary", "hormon", "status",
  offset.name = "rfstime", effect_measure = "IRR",
  adjust_covariates = "ips_covar")

# ITT
res_u <- fn_unadj(df_ps)
res_a <- fn_adj(df_ps)
cat("ITT Estimates:\n")
#> ITT Estimates:

    " (IPS covariate, Bang & Robins 2005)\n")

Note

In the GBSG RCT, PS adjustment has minimal impact because treatment was randomized. The benefit of PS adjustment is most apparent in observational data where confounding is present.

3 Simulation: Confounded Treatment Assignment

To demonstrate the value of PS adjustment, we simulate an observational study where treatment assignment depends on covariates.

3.1 Data-Generating Mechanism

simulate_confounded_trial <- function(n = 2000, seed = 42L) {
  set.seed(seed)

  # Covariates
  x1 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
  x2 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
  x3 <- rnorm(n)
  x4 <- rnorm(n)

  # Confounded treatment: P(W=1) depends on x1 and x3
  ps_true <- plogis(-0.5 + 0.8 * x1 + 0.6 * x3)
  treat   <- rbinom(n, 1, ps_true)

  # True subgroup: x1 == 1
  in_sg <- x1 == 1

  # Outcome: binary event with treatment-subgroup interaction
  # x3 is both a confounder AND a prognostic factor
  lp <- -1.5 + 0.5 * x3 + 0.3 * x4 +
        ifelse(in_sg, 0.8, -0.4) * treat
  event <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp))

  # Follow-up time (for Poisson-offset)
  tte <- rexp(n, rate = 0.05) + 1

  data.frame(
    id = seq_len(n),
    x1 = x1, x2 = x2, x3 = x3, x4 = x4,
    treat = treat, event = event, tte = tte,
    in_sg = in_sg, ps_true = ps_true
  )
}

df_sim <- simulate_confounded_trial(n = 2000, seed = 42L)

cat("Simulated data:\n")
#> Simulated data:
cat("  N =", nrow(df_sim), "\n")
#>   N = 2000
cat("  P(treat=1):", round(mean(df_sim$treat), 3), "\n")
#>   P(treat=1): 0.47
cat("  Event rate:", round(mean(df_sim$event), 3), "\n")
#>   Event rate: 0.209
cat("  True subgroup {x1=1}: n =", sum(df_sim$in_sg),
    sprintf("(%.0f%%)\n", 100 * mean(df_sim$in_sg)))
#>   True subgroup {x1=1}: n = 977 (49%)
cat("\nTrue PS range:", round(range(df_sim$ps_true), 3), "\n")
#> 
#> True PS range: 0.083 0.901
cat("  Mean PS (in_sg=TRUE):", round(mean(df_sim$ps_true[df_sim$in_sg]), 3), "\n")
#>   Mean PS (in_sg=TRUE): 0.561
cat("  Mean PS (in_sg=FALSE):", round(mean(df_sim$ps_true[!df_sim$in_sg]), 3), "\n")
#>   Mean PS (in_sg=FALSE): 0.39

3.4 Monte Carlo Evaluation

Show code 
n_sims <- 100

results <- data.frame(
  sim = integer(), method = character(),
  sg_est = numeric(), co_est = numeric(),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (s in seq_len(n_sims)) {
  df_s <- simulate_confounded_trial(n = 2000, seed = s)
  ps_s <- estimate_propensity_scores(df_s, "treat", confs_sim, method = "grf")
  df_s <- ps_s$data

  fn_u_s <- make_effect_estimator("binary", "treat", "event",
    effect_measure = "OR")
  fn_a_s <- make_effect_estimator("binary", "treat", "event",
    effect_measure = "OR", adjust_covariates = "ips_covar")

  sg_s <- df_s[df_s$x1 == 1, ]
  co_s <- df_s[df_s$x1 == 0, ]

  res_u_sg <- fn_u_s(sg_s)
  res_a_sg <- fn_a_s(sg_s)
  res_u_co <- fn_u_s(co_s)
  res_a_co <- fn_a_s(co_s)

  results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
    sim = s, method = "Unadjusted",
    sg_est = res_u_sg$estimate, co_est = res_u_co$estimate
  ))
  results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
    sim = s, method = "PS-adjusted",
    sg_est = res_a_sg$estimate, co_est = res_a_co$estimate
  ))
}

# Summary statistics
cat("=== Monte Carlo Results (", n_sims, "simulations) ===\n\n")

4 Integration with ForestSearch

4.1 API Usage

# RCT (default: no PS adjustment)
forestsearch(df, outcome_type = "binary", effect_measure = "IRR",
             dmin.grf = 0.0, ...)

# Observational with GRF-based PS (default when is.RCT = FALSE)
forestsearch(df, outcome_type = "binary", effect_measure = "IRR",
             dmin.grf = 0.0, is.RCT = FALSE, ps_method = "grf", ...)

# Observational with LASSO PS
forestsearch(df, outcome_type = "binary", is.RCT = FALSE,
             ps_method = "lasso", ...)

# User-supplied PS
forestsearch(df, outcome_type = "binary", is.RCT = FALSE,
             ps_hat = my_ps_vector, ...)

4.2 Key Design Decisions

  1. IPS covariate, not weight. Following Bang & Robins (2005), the inverse propensity score is included as an adjustment covariate (Y ~ treat + ips_covar) rather than as IPTW. The IPS covariate takes the value \(1/\hat{e}(X)\) for treated and \(1/(1-\hat{e}(X))\) for controls. This gives doubly-robust estimates within each subgroup slice and avoids extreme weight instability in small subgroups.

  2. Full-sample PS used within subgroups. Propensity scores are estimated once on the full sample and carried into subgroup slices as-is. The PS is a design quantity reflecting the treatment assignment mechanism — re-estimating within slices would be methodologically incorrect and statistically unstable.

  3. GRF PS from the screening step. When use_grf = TRUE, the causal forest already estimates W.hat. The grf.subg.harm.glm() function now returns the fitted forest object, enabling PS extraction without re-estimation.

  4. Trimming. PS values are trimmed to [2.5%, 97.5%] before computing the IPS covariate, preventing extreme values from near-zero denominators in subgroup slices where one treatment arm dominates.

  5. Backward compatibility. For is.RCT = TRUE (default), ps_method resolves to "none" and the estimator closure is identical to the unadjusted version. Existing analyses are unaffected.
